title: “YOU REAP WHAT YOU SOW”—BUT IF KARMA WERE THE FINAL WORD, NONE OF US WOULD SURVIVE THE CROSS
paragraphs: “YOU REAP WHAT YOU SOW”—BUT IF KARMA WERE THE FINAL WORD, NONE OF US WOULD SURVIVE THE CROSS

You’ve heard people say, “What goes around comes around.” But what happens when the person who deserves judgment falls at the feet of Jesus? The Bible reveals something far more terrifying than karma—and far more beautiful than getting what you deserve.
There is someone reading this right now who has been quietly waiting for life to punish a person who hurt them.
You don't talk about it much anymore.
You smile. You work. You go to church. You post Bible verses about forgiveness.
But somewhere deep inside, there is a wound that still whispers, One day, God will make them pay.
And maybe there is someone else reading this who is terrified of the opposite.
You are not waiting for someone else's harvest.
You are afraid of your own.
Because you remember what you did.
The lie nobody discovered. The relationship you destroyed. The betrayal you justified. The years you wasted. The sin you kept feeding while telling everyone you were doing fine.
And sometimes, when something painful happens in your life, a frightening thought crosses your mind.
Is God finally making me pay?
If either of those people sounds like you, stay with me.
Because there is a sentence in the Bible that people quote as though it were a spiritual version of karma.
And when you finally understand what the apostle Paul meant, you may never look at your past, your enemies, your suffering, or the cross of Jesus Christ the same way again.
The sentence is found in Galatians 6:7.
“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” — Galatians 6:7, KJV
Those words are real.
They are biblical.
They are serious.
But they do not mean that the universe is keeping a cosmic scoreboard, waiting to deliver every person exactly the suffering or happiness they have earned.
That is where many people misunderstand the difference between biblical sowing and reaping and the popular idea of karma.
And that misunderstanding can do terrible things to a wounded soul.
It can make the hurting person feel cursed.
It can make the prosperous sinner feel untouchable.
It can turn forgiveness into a weakness.
It can make suffering look like evidence of hidden sin.
And worst of all, it can make the cross of Jesus seem unnecessary.
Because if everyone simply receives exactly what they deserve, what room is left for mercy?
What room is left for forgiveness?
What room is left for the scandalous, undeserved, life-transforming grace of God?
Listen carefully.
The Bible does teach that our choices have consequences.
But the Gospel reveals that consequences are not the whole story.
And Jesus Christ is the reason.
In the original Greek of Galatians 6:7, Paul writes:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε, θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται· ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.
Transliterated:
Mē planasthe, theos ou myktērizetai; ho gar ean speirē anthrōpos, touto kai therisei.
A close translation is:
“Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, this also he will reap.”
Notice something important.
Paul does not say the universe cannot be mocked.
He says God is not mocked.
The Greek verb myktērizetai carries the sense of being mocked or treated with contempt.
And the agricultural language is deliberate.
Speirē refers to sowing.
Therisei refers to reaping.
Paul is describing a moral and spiritual reality under the authority of the living God, not an impersonal cosmic mechanism operating independently of Him.
And the next verse makes the context unmistakable.
“For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.” — Galatians 6:8, KJV
Paul is addressing the direction of a person's life.
The flesh, in this context, is not simply the physical body. It refers to fallen human nature operating in rebellion against God.
The Spirit is the Holy Spirit, who gives life and transforms those who belong to Christ.
Paul is warning believers not to deceive themselves into thinking they can cultivate rebellion against God without spiritual consequences.
And he is encouraging them to persevere in doing good, as Galatians 6:9–10 makes clear.
This is not a promise that every good deed will produce wealth, that every bad deed will bring immediate disaster, or that every hardship is repayment for some secret wrongdoing.
It is a call to live before God with eternal seriousness.
And that distinction matters more than you might imagine.
Because somewhere in the world, a faithful mother is burying a child she prayed over every night.
A devoted husband is watching his marriage collapse despite his efforts to save it.
A Christian who tried to do what was right is losing a job while a dishonest coworker gets promoted.
And a woman who has spent years serving God is lying awake, wondering why life has been so merciless.
Imagine walking up to any of them and saying:
Well, you reap what you sow.
Do you hear how cruel that can become?
It takes a biblical warning about moral responsibility and turns it into an accusation against the suffering.
Jesus Himself confronted that kind of thinking.
In John 9, His disciples encountered a man who had been blind from birth.
They asked:
“Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?” — John 9:2, KJV
They assumed someone must have done something wrong.
Somebody had to be responsible.
Somebody had to deserve this.
But Jesus answered:
“Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.” — John 9:3, KJV
Jesus was not declaring that the man or his parents had never sinned. He was rejecting the assumption that this particular blindness resulted from their personal sin.
And suddenly, a whole theology of suspicion begins to collapse.
Not every sickness is punishment.
Not every financial struggle is a curse.
Not every broken relationship is divine revenge.
Not every painful season is God collecting an unpaid debt.
Sometimes we suffer because we live in a fallen world.
Sometimes we suffer because other people sin against us.
Sometimes we experience the natural consequences of our own decisions.
Sometimes we endure trials we cannot fully explain.
And sometimes, as with the man born blind, God's work becomes visible in circumstances that human beings have completely misunderstood.
The book of Job makes the same warning painfully clear.
Job's friends were convinced that suffering must prove wrongdoing.
Their reasoning sounded religious.
Their arguments sounded logical.
But God rebuked them for speaking wrongly about Him (Job 42:7).
Be careful when your theology makes you more eager to explain someone's pain than to sit beside them in it.
Because you may be defending a principle while misrepresenting the heart of God.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to reject that kind of judgment when we are the ones suffering.
It is much harder when the person suffering is someone who hurt us.
Think about the person who betrayed you.
The person who humiliated you.
The person who walked away without apologizing.
The person who seemed to destroy something precious in your life and then continued living as though nothing happened.
You may have said, “I leave it to God.”
But privately, you have imagined the day they would finally feel what you felt.
You wanted them to understand.
You wanted them to regret it.
Maybe you wanted them to hurt.
And you called that justice.

The desire for justice is not automatically sinful. God cares deeply about justice, and Scripture does not require victims to deny evil, abandon appropriate boundaries, or avoid lawful accountability.
But there is a difference between trusting God to judge rightly and secretly making another person's destruction the condition of your peace.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Those words are not permission to pretend wrongdoing never happened.
They are an invitation to release personal vengeance into the hands of the only Judge who sees everything.
God knows what happened.
He knows what was stolen.
He knows what was said behind closed doors.
He knows the tears you wiped away before anyone entered the room.
And He does not need your hatred to help Him remember.
But here is the question that may expose something in all of us.
What if the person who hurt you genuinely repents and God forgives them?
Would you rejoice?
Or would you feel cheated?
That question leads us to one of the most astonishing scenes in the Bible.
A criminal is dying beside Jesus.
He has no time to rebuild his reputation.
No opportunity to spend decades proving he has changed.
No way to undo the crimes that brought him to his execution.
Luke records that one of the criminals acknowledged the justice of their punishment.
“And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss.” — Luke 23:41, KJV
The criminal knew something many of us spend our entire lives avoiding.
He was guilty.
He could not save himself.
And the innocent Jesus was suffering beside him.
Then he turned toward Christ.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42, KJV
That was his plea.
Not a speech about his achievements.
Not a promise that he would compensate everyone he had harmed.
Not a list of religious accomplishments.
Just a guilty man turning to a King whose kingdom he somehow recognized through the blood and humiliation of crucifixion.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43, KJV
Read that again.
The criminal did not escape the earthly consequences of his actions.
He still died on that cross.
But he received a promise of paradise from the Savior he had turned to in faith.
His punishment did not disappear.
Yet his guilt did not have the final word over his eternal destiny.
That is not karma.
That is grace.
And if you have never been deeply disturbed by the mercy of Jesus, perhaps you have not yet realized how desperately you need it yourself.
Because there is another man in Scripture whose story is just as scandalous.
His name was Saul.
He persecuted the church.
He approved of Stephen's death and ravaged Christian households.
He pursued believers as enemies.
And then, on the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus confronted him.
Saul did not meet Christ because he had accumulated enough good deeds to deserve a reward.
He met Christ while moving in the wrong direction.
The persecutor was confronted by the One he persecuted.
And the man who had terrorized believers became the apostle Paul, a servant of the Gospel he once tried to destroy.
Did Paul suddenly live a comfortable life?
No.
He suffered imprisonment, beatings, danger, hardship, and rejection.
Grace did not erase the reality of suffering.
It transformed the direction and purpose of his life.
Paul later wrote:
“This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
The man who wrote about sowing and reaping also knew what it meant to receive mercy he could never earn.
He understood both moral responsibility and divine grace.
He did not teach that salvation comes through earning enough good outcomes.
He taught:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
And immediately afterward, he explained that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because our good works have purchased God's acceptance.
We are saved by grace through faith, and the life of faith bears fruit in obedience.
Good works are not the price of redemption.
They are the fruit of a redeemed life.
This is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to karma with Christian vocabulary.

The popular understanding of karma often imagines a moral cause-and-effect system in which actions bring corresponding consequences. Actual teachings about karma differ among Hindu, Buddhist, and other religious traditions and cannot all be reduced to the slogan “what goes around comes around.”
But biblical sowing and reaping is rooted in the personal, sovereign God of Scripture, His judgment, His patience, His mercy, and His redemptive purposes in Jesus Christ.
It does not operate independently of grace.
And it does not promise that every moral account will be visibly settled before death.
The Bible itself recognizes that wicked people sometimes prosper while righteous people suffer.
Psalm 73 wrestles with that very problem.
The psalmist saw the prosperity of the wicked and nearly stumbled in his faith.
Only when he considered their ultimate end in God's presence did his perspective change.

Ecclesiastes 8:14 likewise acknowledges the disturbing reality that righteous people sometimes experience what seems fitting for the wicked, while wicked people experience what seems fitting for the righteous.
Scripture is not naive about injustice.
It does not pretend that life always looks fair.
Instead, it teaches that God's final judgment is certain even when His present providence is mysterious.
And then the Bible takes us somewhere even more extraordinary.
To a hill outside Jerusalem.
To a wooden cross.
To the place where the only perfectly righteous man who ever lived was condemned as a criminal.
Think about that.
If suffering always proved personal guilt, what would we do with Jesus?
He committed no sin.
Yet He was mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
He was the innocent One suffering for the guilty.
The prophet Isaiah had spoken of this centuries earlier.
In Isaiah 53:5, the Hebrew text includes these words:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ מְדֻכָּא מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ
Transliterated:
Vehu meḥolal mippeshaʿenu, medukka meʿavonotenu.
A close translation is:
“But he was pierced because of our transgressions, crushed because of our iniquities.”
The KJV renders the verse:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
The Hebrew words peshaʿenu and ʿavonotenu refer to our transgressions and our iniquities.
Not His.
Ours.
Christian interpretation understands Isaiah's suffering servant as finding his fulfillment in Jesus Christ, who bore sin and accomplished redemption through His suffering.
And Peter draws that connection explicitly when he writes of Christ bearing our sins in His own body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
Now consider the weight of this.
We have sinned.
God is holy.
Sin deserves judgment.
But Jesus, the sinless Savior, willingly gave Himself for sinners.
As 2 Corinthians 5:21 declares:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
That does not mean Jesus became morally sinful.
It means that the sinless Christ stood in our place in God's saving work so that those united to Him by faith might be reconciled to God.
This is where the language of sowing and reaping must be handled carefully.
It would be too simplistic to say that Jesus merely received a mechanical harvest belonging to someone else.
The cross is not an impersonal transfer of cosmic consequences.
It is the deliberate, loving, saving act of God in Christ.
Justice was not treated as meaningless.
Sin was not declared harmless.
Grace was not cheap.
The Savior gave Himself.
And the resurrection declared that death would not hold Him.
At Calvary, the innocent One suffered for the guilty so that the guilty could be forgiven and made new.
That is the scandal.
That is the grace.
That is why Jesus rewrites everything.
But please do not misunderstand.
Grace is not a spiritual loophole that allows you to keep sowing destruction while demanding a painless harvest.
The same Jesus who forgives sinners calls them to repentance.
The same Gospel that offers pardon also calls us to a transformed life.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether we should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic.
“God forbid.”
A person cannot rightly use the mercy of Christ as an excuse to cultivate the very sins from which Christ came to rescue us.
If you have betrayed someone, repentance may require confession, truthfulness, and appropriate efforts to make restitution.
If you have been dishonest, repentance means turning toward honesty.
If you have harmed others, repentance does not erase their right to safety, accountability, or justice.
If you have destroyed trust, forgiveness does not automatically restore that trust overnight.
And if you are suffering because of decisions you made years ago, coming to Christ does not necessarily remove every earthly consequence.
But it does mean those consequences do not have to define your identity forever.
A prison sentence may remain.
A relationship may not be restored.
A reputation may take years to rebuild.
A scar may remain long after the wound has closed.
Yet in Christ, a repentant sinner can become a new creation.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That is not permission to deny your past.
It is the promise that your past does not have sovereign authority over your future in Christ.
And maybe that is the word you have needed for years.
You keep looking backward.
Back to the person you used to be.
Back to the decision you wish you could undo.
Back to the season when you were far from God.
You remember the shame so vividly that sometimes you wonder whether the Lord remembers you only as the worst version of yourself.
But when you come to Jesus in repentance and faith, you are not asking Him to pretend your sin never happened.
You are trusting the Savior who died and rose again to forgive it.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Those words are not spoken over everyone indiscriminately, regardless of their relationship to Christ.
They are the assurance of those who are in Him.
And what a breathtaking assurance that is.
No condemnation.
Not because you were innocent.
Not because your sin was insignificant.
Not because you suffered enough to pay for it.
But because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that every painful thing happening to you is God's way of making you pay for who you used to be.
You have interpreted every closed door as punishment.
Every disappointment as a sentence.
Every delay as divine anger.
And you have been trying to earn peace through guilt.
But guilt is not a savior.
Self-punishment is not the cross.
And endless shame is not the same thing as repentance.
Godly sorrow leads us toward repentance, as 2 Corinthians 7:10 teaches.
But despair that keeps us hiding from Jesus is not the destination of the Gospel.
Remember Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
He failed publicly, painfully, and personally.
Then he wept bitterly.
But after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and called him to feed His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The denial was real.
The grief was real.
The restoration was real.
Jesus did not call Peter's failure good.
He called Peter back to Himself.
And perhaps the most moving part is that the Lord knew Peter would fail before Peter ever failed.
Yet He had already spoken of praying for him and of Peter strengthening his brothers after turning back (Luke 22:31–32).
What kind of Savior sees the coming failure and still speaks of restoration?
Jesus.
The One who knows everything about us and still calls sinners to repent and come to Him.
Now, there is another side to this message.
And it is for the person who has been treating grace as though it were permission to keep playing with sin.
You cannot plant bitterness every day and expect love to flourish without repentance.
You cannot cultivate deception and expect trust to grow naturally.
You cannot continually feed lust, pride, cruelty, or greed and pretend those habits are spiritually harmless.
What you repeatedly nurture shapes the direction of your life.
Paul's warning is not imaginary.
It is urgent.
The Greek opening of Galatians 6:7, Mē planasthe, means “Do not be deceived.”
It is a warning against self-deception.
You can fool your audience.
You can fool your friends.
You can fool your family.
You may even fool yourself for a while.
But you cannot mock God.
And yet, if the Holy Spirit is exposing sin in your life today, the answer is not to run farther into hiding.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The invitation is not to negotiate with God over how much guilt you must carry.
It is to confess, repent, and trust His mercy through Christ.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
Conviction may be the very means by which God is calling you away from what is destroying you.
And this is where the story of sowing and reaping becomes unexpectedly beautiful.
Because Paul does not only warn us about destructive sowing.
He also calls us to persevere in doing good.
“And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.” — Galatians 6:9, KJV
Maybe you have been sowing prayers nobody hears.
Maybe you have been sowing forgiveness while your heart still aches.
Maybe you have been sowing honesty in a place where dishonesty seems to win.
Maybe you have been sowing kindness while carrying a burden that nobody knows about.
Maybe you have been faithfully teaching your children about Jesus, but you cannot yet see the fruit.
Do not mistake a delayed harvest for an absent God.
Paul does not promise that every prayer will be answered exactly as you imagine or that every faithful act will produce visible success in this life.
But he does encourage believers not to abandon the good they have been called to do.
Faithfulness matters.
Love matters.
Truth matters.
Generosity matters.
Obedience matters.
And no act of genuine faithfulness is hidden from the Lord.
Still, our ultimate hope is not that life will finally reward us with everything we wanted.
Our ultimate hope is Christ Himself.
That distinction protects us from turning Christianity into a transaction.
We do not love God merely so that He will make our lives easier.
We love Him because He first loved us.
We do not give so that heaven will owe us financial prosperity.
We give because we have received grace.
We do not obey to purchase salvation.
We obey because the Savior who redeemed us is worthy.
And that brings us to something very personal.
What are you sowing right now?
Not what are you posting.
Not what do people think about you.
Not what does your church attendance suggest.
What are you cultivating when nobody is watching?
What thoughts are you feeding?
What sins are you excusing?
What grudges are you watering?
What habits are quietly becoming your character?
What truth have you been avoiding because obedience would cost you something?
And what good have you stopped doing because you became tired of waiting?
You do not need to answer publicly to impress anyone.
But you do need to be honest before God.
Because the most dangerous deception is not always believing that sin has no consequences.
Sometimes it is believing that your sin is too great for the mercy of Jesus.
Both lies keep people away from the Savior.
One says, I do not need repentance.
The other says, Repentance will never be enough for someone like me.
The Gospel confronts both.
You need repentance.
And Jesus is a sufficient Savior.
You need grace.
And grace calls you into a new life.
You are responsible for what you sow.
But you are not beyond redemption because of what you have sown.
If this message has touched a place you normally keep hidden, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.

You do not need to expose private details or confess sensitive sins to strangers. God already knows the full story. But sometimes one honest sentence can open the door to encouragement, prayer, and the reminder that you are not walking alone.
And please, think about the person who needs to hear this.
The friend who believes God has abandoned them because life has become painful.
The brother who has been running from Jesus because of shame.
The sister who is struggling to forgive someone who hurt her.
The parent who feels that years of faithful prayer have been wasted.
The believer who has confused suffering with divine rejection.
Perhaps that day will come sooner than you think.
There is a reason we continue building Gospel Warrior.
Not because we believe another page, ministry, or personality can replace the local church, the Word of God, or the saving work of Jesus Christ.

But because the Gospel deserves to be proclaimed faithfully, and people need continual encouragement to open their Bibles, examine their lives, repent of sin, and grow in the grace and knowledge of the Lord.
Every article takes work.
Every biblical explanation requires care.
Every resource we make available is an opportunity to help someone move beyond a passing emotional moment toward a deeper life of discipleship.
Not out of guilt.
Not because a monthly payment earns God's favor.
And certainly not because financial support is a substitute for the tithes and offerings you prayerfully give through your local church.
You cannot buy grace. You cannot purchase spiritual maturity. And you do not owe a ministry money in order to prove your love for Jesus.
Think of it as becoming a faithful partner in the work, according to your ability and conviction.
Philippians 4:15–18 describes believers supporting Paul's ministry through their giving. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not pressured or grudging.
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
Your prayers matter.
Your faithful encouragement matters.
You can help without spending a single peso or dollar.
Those products are not the reason to give.
Those resources are there to encourage serious growth in Jesus Christ through biblical reading, prayer, spiritual reflection, and practical discipleship.
Jesus Christ.
The One who did not come to flatter sinners, but to save them.
The One who did not minimize sin, but bore its cost.
The One who calls us to repent, believe, follow, and become new.
And before you leave this article, I want to return to the question we began with.
What happens when the person who deserves judgment falls at the feet of Jesus?
Sometimes there are still consequences.
Sometimes there are still tears.
Sometimes restitution is necessary.
Sometimes relationships remain broken.
Sometimes healing takes years.
But for the one who truly turns to Christ in repentance and faith, there is forgiveness.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is the gift of the Holy Spirit.
There is a new direction.
There is hope beyond the grave.
And there is a Savior whose resurrection is greater than the power of death.
The world may tell you that your life is nothing more than the sum of what you have done.
Your shame may tell you that you will never escape the person you used to be.
Your bitterness may tell you that peace will only come when the person who hurt you finally suffers enough.
But Jesus calls you to something different.
Repent.
Believe.
Forgive as you have been forgiven.
Pursue justice without becoming consumed by vengeance.
Sow to the Spirit.
Do not grow weary in doing good.
And trust the God who is both perfectly just and astonishingly merciful.
You reap what you sow.
Yes, that is biblical.
But do not stop reading Scripture at the warning.
Keep reading until you reach the cross.
Keep reading until you reach the empty tomb.
Keep reading until you hear the promise that those who belong to Christ are no longer under condemnation.
Keep reading until you understand that Christianity is not about an impersonal universe giving you exactly what you have earned.
It is about the living God calling sinners to repentance and offering eternal life through His Son.
And if you remember nothing else from these words, remember this:
Your sin was serious enough that Jesus went to the cross—but His grace is sufficient to save everyone who comes to Him in faith.
So stop treating karma as your judge.
Stop treating shame as your identity.
Stop treating revenge as your healing.
And stop treating grace as permission to remain unchanged.
Come to Jesus.
The real Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The Savior who forgives.
The King who transforms.
The One who takes people whose stories seem ruined and makes them living testimonies of His mercy.
Because the most unforgettable part of your story does not have to be what you did, what someone did to you, or what you lost.
It can be what Jesus Christ did to redeem you.
The scars may still tell the story of what happened—but they do not get to write the final sentence when your life belongs to Jesus.
